CONTEXT: Treaty-as-code where ratification = two sovereign implementations independently deriving an identical Merkle root over the clause tree. The threat model is not adversaries but divergence: map iteration order, Unicode normalization drift, float formatting, omitted-vs-empty fields, timezone-local dates, and "lenient" parsers. Every one of these has broken real cross-implementation systems.
ROLE: Protocol designer producing a normative, implementable specification.
TASK: Specify canonical encoding "TXC-1" end-to-end — field order, encodings, normalization, hashing — such that two independent teams converge byte-for-byte.
CONSTRAINTS: Normative numbered rules (MUST/SHALL); no vague operators ("sort appropriately" is banned); no fabricated hash values; unverifiable steps flagged; density over padding.
INPUTS: Prompt only. External anchors: FIPS 180-4 (SHA-256), RFC 8032 (Ed25519), RFC 6962 (Merkle structure precedent), UAX #15 (NFC).
SUCCESS: Two teams sharing no code, given this spec plus frozen test vectors, produce identical roots on positive vectors and identical accept/reject verdicts on negative vectors.
OUTPUT: Spec TXC-1 below.

---

# TXC-1 — Canonical Treaty Encoding, v1

## 1. Design principles (drive every rule below)

- **P1 — Normalize once, verify strictly forever.** All normalization (Unicode, newlines, decimals) happens exactly once, at authoring. Verifiers NEVER re-normalize; they validate canonicality and reject violations. Two validators agreeing on rejections is far easier than two normalizers agreeing on transformations. This is the load-bearing decision.
- **P2 — Totality.** Every field is always present, in schema-declaration order, at fixed width. No omission, no defaults, no `omitempty`. Absence is encoded (`Option` tag).
- **P3 — Reject, don't repair.** Any violation ⇒ fail closed, no output.
- **P4 — Tagged and length-prefixed everywhere.** No value is parseable two ways.
- **P5 — Sort by content order, never by encoded-byte order.** (Encoded-byte comparison sorts `"b"` before `"aa"` via length prefixes — a classic divergence bug.)
- **P6 — Pin every external dependency** (Unicode version, hash, curve, calendar, language registry) and bind the format version into the root.
- **P7 — Conformance is behavioral:** byte-identical outputs on frozen vectors, including negative vectors.

## 2. Artifact envelope

```
offset  size  field
0       4     magic = "TXC1" (0x54 58 43 31)
4       2     format_version = 0x0001 (u16be)
6       4     payload_length (u32be)
10      ...   payload (single TLV composite, tag 0x20 Header-rooted document)
```
Trailing bytes after `payload_length` ⇒ reject. BOM anywhere ⇒ reject.

## 3. Primitive encodings

All integers big-endian, fixed width per tag. No varints, no floats, ever.

| Tag | Type | Encoding | Constraints |
|-----|------|----------|-------------|
| 0x01 | u8 | 1 byte | — |
| 0x02 | u16 | 2 bytes BE | — |
| 0x03 | u32 | 4 bytes BE | — |
| 0x04 | u64 | 8 bytes BE | — |
| 0x05 | i64 | 8 bytes BE two's complement | — |
| 0x06 | utf8 | u32be byte-len + bytes | see §4 |
| 0x07 | bytes | u32be byte-len + bytes | — |
| 0x08 | bool | 1 byte | 0x00 or 0x01 only |
| 0x09 | decimal | u32be len + ASCII | grammar `-?(0\|[1-9][0-9]*)(\.[0-9]+)?`; no exponent, no `+`, no `-0`, no leading zeros |
| 0x0A | date | u32be days since 1970-01-01, proleptic Gregorian, UTC | range 0001-01-01..9999-12-31 |
| 0x0C | option | 0x00 (none) \| 0x01 + one TLV value | — |
| 0x0D | array | u32be count + count full TLV elements | count ≤ schema max |
| 0x20+ | composite | u32be payload-len + fields in declaration order | tags assigned by this spec |

Reserved: 0x00, 0x0B, 0x0E–0x1F. Unknown tag ⇒ reject (closed world; evolution = version bump).

## 4. Text (authoring-time normalization, then frozen)

Applied once when the canonical artifact is produced:
1. Decode source as strict UTF-8: reject overlongs, surrogates, >U+10FFFF.
2. Strip U+FEFF if (illegally) present, then reject any remaining BOM.
3. Normalize to **NFC, Unicode 15.0.0 exactly** (pinned; bump = version bump).
4. Line endings: CRLF and CR → LF. Strip trailing spaces/tabs per line. No other whitespace alteration (internal spacing may carry quotation fidelity).
5. Allowed controls: U+000A only. All other C0/C1 ⇒ reject.

Verifier duties: strict UTF-8 decode, NFC quick-check against pinned tables, control-character scan. It does not transform anything.

## 5. Collections and sorting

- Encoders MUST sort before encoding; validators MUST verify adjacent-element order (O(n)).
- Ordering per element type: utf8 → unsigned byte-lexicographic of the string content (identical to codepoint order — a UTF-8 property); integers/dates → numeric; composites → by their schema-designated sort-key field.
- Duplicates (full canonical-encoding equality) ⇒ reject. Sort+dedup is mandatory, not stylistic.
- Empty arrays permitted only where schema declares min=0. Treaty ≥1 article; article ≥1 clause (this deliberately sidesteps the empty-Merkle-tree convention debate).

## 6. Document schema (field order is normative)

```
Header(0x20):     format_version u16 · treaty_id utf8(ASCII slug) ·
                  title Array<LangText> · parties Array<Party> ·
                  amends Option<bytes32> · created Date
Party(0x21):      code u16 · name Array<LangText> · ed25519_pubkey bytes[32]
LangText(0x22):   lang u16 (closed enum, appendix: eng=1, fra=2, …) · body utf8
Clause(0x23):     id utf8 (pattern ^A\d{3}\.C\d{3}(\.S\d{3})$, zero-padded so
                    byte-sort == numeric-sort) ·
                  kind u16 enum {1 obligation, 2 right, 3 definition,
                    4 procedure, 5 dispute, 6 amendment, 7 annex-ref} ·
                  texts Array<LangText> (min 1, sort by lang) ·
                  refs Array<utf8> (clause ids, sorted, deduped, must resolve) ·
                  effective Option<Date> · conditions Array<utf8> (sorted)
Article(0x24):    number u16 · title Array<LangText> · clauses Array<Clause>
                    (min 1, sort by id)
Annex(0x25):      id utf8 ("X%03d") · title Array<LangText> · body Array<LangText>
```
Closed language enum replaces BCP-47 canonicalization entirely — one less normalizer to agree on. New languages = version bump. Clause IDs are immutable post-ratification; amendments are new documents with `amends = prior_root` and full restatement (no deltas — delta application is a divergence machine).

## 7. Hash tree (the root)

Domain-separated SHA-256 throughout:

```
clause_leaf(a,c) = SHA256(0x00 || tlv(Clause))
pair(l,r)        = SHA256(0x02 || l || r)
M([x])           = x
M(xs)            = M(pairs(xs))          # odd count ⇒ duplicate last child (pinned, RFC 6962-style)
article_node     = SHA256(0x01 || u32be(k_clauses) || M(clause_leaves))
header_node      = SHA256(0x04 || tlv(Header))
annex_node       = SHA256(0x06 || tlv(Annex))
ROOT             = SHA256(0x07 || u32be(n_top) ||
                          M([header_node] ++ article_nodes ++ annex_nodes))
```

Subtree sizes are bound inside preimages (kills second-preimage/framing ambiguities). Depth cap 64; string cap 1 MiB; counts capped per schema. Human display: lowercase hex, 64 chars; wire: 32 raw bytes.

## 8. Ratification receipts

Each sovereign signs the root it derived:

```
msg_i = 0x03 || ROOT(32) || u16be(party_code) || u32be(created_days)
sig_i = Ed25519(pure, RFC 8032, NO context string, NO prehash) over msg_i   # 64 bytes
```

Pure Ed25519 is deterministic by construction — no nonce-divergence class exists. Verification MUST follow RFC 8032 decoding and reject malleable signatures (S ≥ L). Keys live in the Header, so anyone can verify receipts offline. Depositary record = composite `{root bytes32, receipts Array<Receipt{code u16, date Date, sig bytes64}>}` — post-ratification, outside the tree.

**Dispute localization protocol:** exchange `article_node` hashes; first differing index localizes the divergence to one article; exchange that article's clause leaves; the differing leaf is the divergent clause. The Merkle structure doubles as the debugging protocol.

## 9. Validator checklist (all fail-closed)

reasoning:
Let me parse this request carefully. The user wants a canonical serialization scheme for a "two-sovereign treaty as code" — a treaty between two sovereign entities (states, organizations) encoded in a deterministic data structure where:

1. Matching roots = ratified clauses (i.e., the Merkle root of the clause tree serves as the ratification fingerprint — if both parties compute the same root, the treaty text is identical and ratified)
2. The scheme must make TWO independent implementations produce byte-identical roots from the same start
3. Need exact field ordering, encoding, normalization rules
4. Concrete, implementable

This is a real engineering problem: canonical serialization for cross-implementation determinism. The classic pitfalls:
- Map/dict iteration order (must sort keys)
- Unicode normalization (NFC vs NFD), string encoding (UTF-8)
- Integer widths, endianness
- Float representation (ban floats or use fixed-point)
- Optional fields / null handling
- Duplicate keys
- Whitespace/newline normalization in human-readable text
- Hash function choice (SHA-256 is safe)
- Length-prefixing to avoid ambiguity
- Domain separation tags to prevent type confusion / cross-protocol attacks
- Versioning of the serialization format itself
- Handling of arrays vs sets (arrays ordered by position; sets sorted canonically)
- Timestamps (normalize to UTC epoch seconds or ISO 8601 with fixed precision)
- Legal citation formats — clauses reference each other by ID
- Signature blocks — signatures over the root, not over serialized bytes that might differ

The design should be a TLV (tag-length-value) binary format or a canonical JSON profile. For a treaty-as-code with two independent implementations needing byte-identical output, a strict binary TLV is actually easier to make deterministic than canonical JSON (fewer edge cases: no number formatting issues, no string escaping ambiguity). But canonical JSON is more human-auditable. Best answer: define a binary core (for hashing/root computation) plus a human-readable source form that compiles deterministically into the binary form. Actually, let me think about what's most implementable and defensible.

The key insight from the domain: this resembles RFC 8785 (JCS - JSON Canonicalization Scheme), CBOR canonical forms (RFC 8949 Section 4.2), and certificate transparency / Merkle tree designs (RFC 6962). Also UDI/UNID for legal documents. The treaty structure: Preamble, Parties, Articles → Clauses → Sub-clauses, Definitions, Annexes, Signatures.

Design decisions I need to make explicitly:

1. **Hash**: SHA-256. Leaf = H(0x00 || encoded_clause); internal node = H(0x01 || left || right). Domain separation per RFC 6962 style. Root = 32 bytes.

2. **Encoding**: Deterministic binary TLV. Tag byte(s), length as varint or fixed 4-byte big-endian, value. Big-endian everywhere. UTF-8 strings, NFC-normalized... wait, NFC normalization is itself an implementation hazard (Unicode version drift). Two independent implementations using different Unicode versions could normalize differently. Mitigation: pin Unicode version in the spec, AND include the codepoint sequence check. Actually the safest approach for cross-implementation identity: restrict the character repertoire (e.g., allow only specific ranges), require NFC with pinned Unicode version, and reject non-conforming input rather than silently normalizing. Better: normalize at authoring time, store normalized bytes, and verification only checks that stored bytes are already NFC (idempotence check) — so verifiers don't need a full normalizer, just a validator. Hmm, but validating NFC still needs tables. Alternative: define the canonical form as "the exact UTF-8 byte sequence as authored after a single normalization pass at compile time" and have the root computed over those bytes; both implementations hash the same compiled artifact. The risk is only when two implementations compile from source independently. So: pin Unicode 15.0.0 NFC, forbid unassigned codepoints, forbid control chars except none, normalize line endings to LF, strip trailing whitespace per line, collapse... no — collapsing whitespace changes legal meaning? In treaties, whitespace isn't semantically meaningful usually, but let's be careful: define exactly one whitespace policy: lines split on \n, CRLF→LF, trailing spaces stripped, no leading-space changes (indentation may be semantic in structured fields but in prose it isn't — keep it simple: strip trailing, collapse internal runs of spaces/tabs to single space? That could alter quoted text. Safer: CRLF→LF + strip trailing whitespace per line + NFC + forbid other controls. Don't collapse internal spaces.)

3. **Numbers**: Integers only, big-endian two's complement with minimal-width rule? Minimal-width causes implementation variance (some encoders emit 4 bytes always). Rule: fixed widths per field type defined by schema — u16 for enum-ish, u32 for ordinals, i64 for timestamps... Actually simplest deterministic rule: every integer field has a schema-declared fixed width and signedness. No varints (varint rules are well-defined but add complexity; fixed width is trivially deterministic). Ban floats entirely; monetary/ratio values as {units: i64, scale: u32} rational pairs or decimal strings with a strict grammar (digits, optional fraction, no exponent, no leading zeros except "0", no "+", "-0" forbidden).

4. **Strings**: UTF-8, NFC (pinned Unicode version), length-prefixed with u32 byte length, forbidden: surrogates (CESU/WTF-8 rejection), C1 controls, C0 except nothing (all C0 forbidden since we normalize newlines away before encoding — actually keep \n inside multi-line text fields? If we store prose as a single string with embedded \n, then \n is allowed. Let me allow \n only.)

5. **Structures**: Schema-driven. Every composite has a tag. Field order = declaration order in the schema (fixed by spec, not by encoder). No optional fields — use explicit presence enums or default values materialized (absence must be encoded, not skipped, to avoid "omit vs empty" divergence). This is important: optional-field omission is a huge source of divergence. Rule: every field always present; nullable via explicit Option<T> tag (0x00 = None, 0x01 = Some(v)).

6. **Maps**: Only sorted maps allowed; sort by NFC-normalized key bytes, lexicographic unsigned byte comparison of UTF-8. Duplicates = error. Or avoid maps entirely in favor of sorted arrays of key-value pairs. Sorted array of pairs is more explicit. Use that.

7. **Sets**: sorted arrays, dedup required, sort order defined per element type (byte-lexicographic on their canonical encoding).

8. **Tree shape**: Treaty = list of Articles; Article = list of Clauses; Clause has stable ID (e.g., "ART3.CL7"), ordinal, kind (obligation/right/definition/procedure/amendment-rule/dispute), text, references (sorted list of clause IDs), effective dates, conditions. Merkleize: leaf per clause; article nodes = Merkle over clause leaves; root = Merkle over article nodes with counts bound (bind subtree sizes to prevent second-preimage/fractional-tree ambiguities — bind the count in the internal node preimage).

9. **Ratification record**: Each party signs H("TREATY-RATIFY-v1" || root || party_id || timestamp). Signature algorithm pinned: Ed25519 (RFC 8032) over the 32-byte message... Ed25519 signs messages directly; fine. Or ECDSA P-256 with RFC 6979 deterministic nonce (determinism matters! RFC 6979 mandatory). Pin one. Ed25519 simpler, deterministic by construction. Point encoding: compressed y with sign bit, standard.

10. **Versioning**: Format version byte in the header; the root binds the version. Any change to normalization rules ⇒ version bump ⇒ different roots (intentional).

11. **Test vectors**: Mandatory conformance vectors — a fixed treaty fixture with expected intermediate hashes and final root, hex-encoded. Two implementations are conformant iff they reproduce all vectors byte-for-byte. Include adversarial vectors: NFD input must be rejected-or-normalized identically, duplicate map keys rejected, float rejected, etc.

12. **Ambiguity kills**: 
    - Length prefixes everywhere → no concatenation ambiguity.
    - Tags on every value → no type confusion.
    - Explicit terminator not needed with lengths.
    - Nested length limits (max depth 64, max string 1 MiB, max clauses 65,535) to bound DoS.
    
13. **What about the "two-sovereign" aspect**: Party A and Party B each run their own implementation ("sovereign stacks"). Ratification protocol: both compute root locally from their own codebase; exchange roots out-of-band (diplomatic channel); equality ⇒ texts match ⇒ sign. Dispute resolution: recompute from canonical source; if roots differ, bisect by article subtrees (each article node hash exchanged) to localize divergence — nice operational touch: the Merkle structure doubles as a diff-debug protocol.

14. **Timestamps**: Unix epoch seconds, i64, UTC only. No sub-second (or fixed millis). Dates (legal effective dates) as day-granularity: days since epoch or YYYY-MM-DD packed u32 (year*10000+month*100+day as u32 — simple, sortable).

15. **Enums**: u16 codes, registry in spec appendix, unknown = hard error (no forward-compat leniency — leniency breaks determinism across versions; version byte handles evolution instead).

16. **Language/multilingual**: Treaties often authentic in two languages. Model: clause has `texts: sorted array of {lang: BCP-47 lowercase canonical form (e.g., "en", "fr"), body: string}`. Canonical lang tag: lowercase, subtags joined with "-", canonicalized per IANA registry pinned date. Simpler: restrict to ISO 639-1/639-3 primary + optional region per pinned registry; sort by lang tag bytes.

17. **Byte-order mark**: forbidden in inputs; reject EF BB BF.

18. **The compile pipeline** (source → canonical): 
    Source (YAML/DSL) → parse → validate against schema → normalize (Unicode NFC pinned, newline, whitespace policy, decimal grammar) → encode TLV → hash tree → root. Both sovereigns may author in their own tooling but must produce the canonical artifact; better practice: the canonical artifact itself (the TLV blob) is exchanged and hashed, so hashing never re-runs normalization. Normalization happens once, at drafting; verification validates canonicality (rejects non-canonical) rather than re-normalizing. This asymmetry (normalize-once, verify-strictly) is THE key trick for cross-implementation determinism: it converts a hard problem (two normalizers agreeing) into an easy one (two validators rejecting the same malformed inputs). Validators are much easier to make agree than normalizers. I should foreground this principle.

Wait — but validators still need NFC validation which needs Unicode tables. Pinning Unicode version makes tables finite and testable; also provide the conformance vectors covering tricky cases (combining sequences, Hangul, singleton mappings like U+212B Å → U+00C5). Alternatively forbid combining characters entirely?? Too restrictive for French/Spanish legal text? Precomposed forms cover most Latin diacritics (é = U+00E9 exists), but e.g., Vietnamese has some decomposed-only sequences? Vietnamese uses precomposed Latin Extended Additional mostly (ế U+1EBF exists). Devanagari inherently uses combining marks (virama) — can't forbid combining marks for Hindi. So: allow combining marks, pin NFC, provide vectors. Fine.

19. **Deterministic error behavior**: On any validation failure, implementations must fail closed (no output). Never "best-effort fix."

20. **Root computation spec, precise**:
```
leaf(i)        = SHA256(0x00 || encode(Clause_i))
node(children) = SHA256(0x01 || u64be(n_children) || fold(children))
fold([c])      = c
fold(cs)       = fold(pairwise(cs))   -- pairwise: h = SHA256(0x02 || left || right)
```

  where M over odd counts duplicates last? RFC 6962 duplicates last on odd. Duplication creates known ambiguity concerns but is fine if pinned. Alternative: always pad with zero-hash to power of two? Padding with zeros is also fine if pinned. Choose: odd ⇒ duplicate last child (RFC 6962 style), pinned.
- Treaty root R = SHA256(0x02 || u32be(num_articles) || M(A_1..A_m)) with same odd-duplication.
Domain-separation constants: 0x00 leaf, 0x01 article, 0x02 root, 0x03 ratification receipt, 0x04 annex. Clean.

Also bind the header into the root? The root should commit to everything: header (version, treaty_id, parties) should be part of the tree — make header a pseudo-article 0 or hash it into root preimage: R = SHA256(0x02 || u32be(m) || M(A...) ) and separately R' = SHA256(0x03 || header_hash || R)? Simplest: top-level Merkle over [HeaderNode, ArticleNodes..., AnnexNodes...] where HeaderNode = SHA256(0x04 || TLV(Header)). Then root commits to everything. Good.

21. **Canonical TLV wire format precise**:
- Tag: single byte for primitives (0x01 u8, 0x02 u16, 0x03 u32, 0x04 u64, 0x05 i64, 0x06 str, 0x07 bytes, 0x08 bool, 0x09 decimal, 0x0A date, 0x0B null/none marker, 0x10+ composites per schema registry).
- Composite: tag byte (schema-assigned, ≥0x20), u32be payload length, payload = concatenation of fields in schema declaration order, each field itself TLV-encoded.
- Top-level document: magic "TXC1" (treaty exchange canonical v1) + u16be format_version=1 + u32be total_len + payload. Magic guards against feeding wrong files.
- Bool: 0x00 false, 0x01 true, other = invalid.
- Decimal: grammar `-?(0|[1-9][0-9]*)(\.[0-9]+)?`, encoded as str-tagged? Give own tag 0x09 with the ASCII bytes, validated by regex-equivalent state machine. Value semantics: exact decimal, scale = digits after point; comparisons defined but not needed for hashing.
- Date: u32be days-since-1970-01-01 (proleptic Gregorian). Range check 0001-01-01..9999-12-31.
- Strings: tag 0x06, u32be byte-length, UTF-8 bytes (already normalized & validated).
- Arrays: not a generic tag; they appear as composites with u32be count prefix then elements. Define ArrayOf<T> encoding: u32be(count) || elements each fully TLV'd. Count bounds per schema.
- Sorted structures: sort key = raw byte comparison of the element's full TLV encoding? Careful: byte-compare of TLV encodings sorts by tag first then length then content — for homogeneous arrays tags equal, so effectively length-then-bytes, which differs from content-lexicographic ("b" < "aa" by length-first!). That's a trap. Fix: sorting rule = compare by the *value* ordering defined per type: strings by UTF-8 byte lexicographic of the string content (not including length prefix); clause IDs likewise; integers numeric. State explicitly: "sort by content ordering of the element type, NOT by encoded-byte comparison." Good catch — this is exactly the kind of divergence bug that bites dual implementations.

22. **Clause ID scheme**: "A{article:03d}.C{clause:03d}[.S{sub:03d}]" — fixed-width zero-padded, ASCII only, unique, immutable once ratified (amendments add new IDs or supersede via pointer, never mutate). References stored as sorted deduped array of these IDs; dangling reference = validation error.

23. **Amendment model**: Treaty is immutable; amendment = new treaty document with `amends: [prior_root]` field and full restated text (restatement-in-full avoids delta-application divergence). Prior root referenced as 32-byte hex? As bytes field.

24. **Conformance harness**: vectors file = JSON? No — vectors distributed as hex blobs + expected hashes, with a plain-text manifest. Provide ~20 vectors: empty treaty, single clause, unicode stress (Å, 한글 decomposition, emoji ZWJ), long text, max-depth nesting, duplicate-key rejection, bad-UTF8 rejection, float rejection, CRLF input, BOM rejection, odd-count merkle duplication case, etc. Implementations must assert rejections too.

25. **Two-sovereign protocol steps** (operational): 
  1. Drafters produce canonical artifact C (TLV blob) + root R.
  2. Exchange C over authenticated channel; each side independently validates C (strict validator) and recomputes R'. 
  3. R == R' ⇒ text agreed. 
  4. Each sovereign signs receipt Sig_i = Ed25519(sign_key_i, 0x03 || R || u16be(party_code) || date). 
  5. Receipts exchanged; combined receipt pair appended to depositary record. 
  6. Any later dispute: re-validate artifact; artifact is the treaty (bytes are the law — "meet at the bytes").
  
This matches the standing invariant "meet at the bytes and the structure, not the gloss."

Anti-goals: no JSON for hashing (JCS exists but number/string escaping edge cases and two JSON parsers agreeing is harder than two TLV validators); no XML; no floats; no locale-dependent anything; no timezone-local dates; no implicit defaults; no "omitempty"; no varint (keep fixed widths); no re-normalization at verify time.

Also mention: why not just RFC 8785 JCS? Because our domain needs binary stability, fixed schemas, and rejection semantics; JCS is fine for JSON ecosystems but pins ES6 number formatting — implementing Number::toString identically in two languages is notoriously fiddly. Our format bans floats so the whole class dies. Worth one line.

Key design principles to headline:
P1. Normalize once at authoring; verify strictly thereafter (never re-normalize at verify). Converts agreement-on-transformations into agreement-on-rejections.
P2. Total functional totality: every field present, fixed order, fixed width, no omission.
P3. Reject, don't repair.
P4. Everything length-prefixed and tagged; no context-free ambiguity.
P5. Content-ordering for sorts, not encoding-ordering.
P6. Pin every external dependency (Unicode version, hash, curve, date system) in the header/spec; version byte bumps on any change.
P7. Conformance = byte-identical outputs on shared vectors, including negative vectors.
